## Ezra 7 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — “Many years later, during the reign of Artaxerxes…”

The phrase “Now after these things” (or “Many years later”) marks the only use of this distinctive phrase in Ezra, signalling a major transition. The interval between the temple completion (Ezra 6, under Darius I) and Ezra’s arrival is about 57–58 years. The Artaxerxes here is Artaxerxes I Longimanus (r. 464–423 BC), grandson of Darius I and son of Xerxes (the king who married Esther). The events of Esther fall in this gap. His 7th year would be 458/457 BC. Some older interpreters (Jarchi, Aben Ezra, and Gill) equated this Artaxerxes with Darius of the preceding chapter, but most modern conservative scholars distinguish them. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

### vv. 1–5 — Ezra’s Genealogy

The genealogy traces Ezra back to “Aaron the chief priest” through the line of Eleazar, Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki, Uzzi, Zerahiah, Meraioth, Azariah, Amariah, Ahitub, Zadok, Shallum, Hilkiah, Azariah, and Seraiah. The list is not exhaustive — about six names are omitted between Azariah and Meraioth (compare 1 Chronicles 6:3–15), and a Meraioth is likely omitted between Zadok and Ahitub (cf. 1 Chronicles 9:11). This telescoping is common in biblical genealogies: every descendant is a “son” and every ancestor a “father.” Seraiah was the last high priest to minister in Solomon’s temple, executed by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah (2 Kings 25:18–21), making Ezra his great-grandson or great-great-grandson. Hilkiah was the high priest under Josiah who discovered the Book of the Law (2 Kings 22:4–14). Zadok was the priest under David whose line held the high priesthood until 171 BC; the Sadducees and the Qumran community both looked back to Zadok. The genealogy establishes Ezra’s priestly credentials and prepares the reader for a man of considerable importance. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### v. 6 — “This Ezra came up from Babylon…”

**“He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses.”** The Hebrew word translated “skilled” (or “ready”) means literally “rapid” (cf. Psalm 45:1), suggesting quickness of grasp and ease amid complex material — the fruit of devoted study (described in v. 10). A scribe in this era was not a mere secretary or copyist; he was an expert interpreter, teacher, and administrator of the Law — a role akin to a highly trained lawyer in God’s Word. Kidner says Ezra “stamped Israel with its lasting character as the people of a book.” Scribes had three main functions: to preserve, to teach, and to administer (interpret and apply) the Word of God. By Jesus’ day, many scribes had degenerated into opponents of His ministry (Matthew 7:29; 23), but Ezra was the ideal — the founder and type of the new order. Note that the verse describes the Law as “which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given” — showing that Ezra did not see himself as a reviser or compiler but as a steward of something divinely given. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

**“The king had granted Ezra all his requests, for the hand of the LORD his God was upon him.”** This is the first of three occurrences of “the hand of the LORD” in this chapter (also vv. 9, 28). The phrase recurs five more times in Ezra–Nehemiah. It denotes God’s special providence, favour, and blessing. The king’s generosity is attributed entirely to God’s sovereign influence over the monarch’s heart. Matthew Henry comments: “Every creature is that to us which God makes it to be. We must see the hand of God in the events that befall us.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### v. 7 — “In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes…”

The same six classes listed as returning with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:70) are named here: Israelites, priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants (Nethinim). The date — the seventh year of Artaxerxes I — is 458/457 BC. This is the first of several precise chronological markers. Gill notes that some of the ten tribes may have been among those returning, having stayed in Babylon until they saw how matters in Judea prospered. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html)

### vv. 8–9 — The Journey: Four Months

Ezra arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month (Ab, roughly July–August) of the seventh year, having departed Babylon on the first day of the first month (Nisan, roughly March–April). The journey took exactly four months. The direct distance is about 500 miles, but the route likely followed the Euphrates northwest then south, totalling about 900 miles. A caravan with families, goods, and livestock required many rest days (one such rest was at Ahava, Ezra 8:15). Ellicott observes: the journey “comes afterwards” in the narrative — here it is summarised beforehand, according to the manner of the book. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html)

**“For the gracious hand of his God was upon him.”** The second mention of the “hand of God.” Kidner notes that this brief summary “gives no hint of the initial disappointment and delay, the fasting and prayer, and the dangers of such a journey, which will emerge in the full account” (Ezra 8). The safe four-month journey is attributed to God’s good hand, not to human planning or Persian protection. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### v. 10 — “For Ezra had set his heart to study… practice… teach”

This is the theological key to the chapter. The “good hand of his God” upon Ezra (v. 9) is explained by this verse: Ezra had prepared (or “set,” “fixed,” “determined”) his heart with a threefold purpose:

1. **To study (seek) the Law of the LORD.** To “seek” the law is to aim at a complete, deep knowledge — not casual reading but diligent inquiry. As Matthew Henry says, he “made it his business to inquire into it, searched the scriptures, and sought the knowledge of God.”

2. **To practice (do) it.** Knowledge must lead to obedience. Clarke comments: “He prepares, he fixes, purposes, and determines, with his heart … to seek the law of God, and to do it himself, that he may be properly qualified to teach.” Without personal practice, teaching becomes hypocrisy.

3. **To teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel.** Statutes (*chuqqim*) refer to positive ceremonial enactments; judgments/ordinances (*mishpatim*) refer to moral precepts. The full impact of God’s Word is made when it is sought, lived, and then passed on to others.

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that God’s favour towards Ezra and the prosperous issue of his journey were the *consequences* of his having set his heart on these things — not as a reward, but as the divinely ordered result. Ellicott adds: “It must be remembered that the providence of God over him immediately precedes — not as the reward of his preparing his heart, but as the reason of it.”

Trapp’s older comment: “An instrument must be tuned ere it can be played upon; sour wines need good sweetening.” The Living Bible paraphrases: “Ezra had determined to study and obey the laws of the Lord and to become a Bible teacher.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezra-7.html)

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** “Every period of reformation in history begins with a return to sacred Scripture, and this was as true in Ezra’s day as it was in the Protestant Reformation … Ezra is a model for how the church should study Scripture and apply it in a way that fosters reformation.” One commentator notes that if Ezra could esteem the Torah — only a portion of Scripture — we should be much more eager to plumb the depths of the completed canon. Ligonier also stresses that personal Bible study is rooted in this Old Testament pattern. [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/studying-doing-and-teaching](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/studying-doing-and-teaching)

### v. 11 — “This is the text of the letter…”

The letter (vv. 11–26) is written in Aramaic, the diplomatic language of the Persian Empire. Ezra is described as “the priest and scribe, an expert in the commandments and statutes of the LORD to Israel.” Ellicott notes that the function of scribe was more important than that of priest in Ezra’s case: he was the expositor of both general moral commandments and special ceremonial statutes — and it was “with the latter more especially that the commission of Ezra had to do.” The letter is from Ezra’s own hand, and throughout we can discern his own phrasing. [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/7-11.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezra/7-11.htm)

### v. 12 — “Artaxerxes, king of kings…”

The title “king of kings” was inherited by Persian monarchs from the Babylonians (cf. Daniel 2:37). Ellicott notes it is used only by the king himself, not by the narrator. “Greetings” (or “perfect peace”) — the Hebrew/Aramaic is literally “perfect, and so forth.” The apocryphal Esdras supplies “peace,” which traditional translations follow. Gill takes “perfect” as referring to Ezra’s qualification as a “most learned and complete scribe.” [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

---

### vv. 13–14 — The Decree: Volunteers and Commission

**v. 13:** The decree permits any Israelite volunteer — including priests and Levites — to accompany Ezra. It does not compel; it opens the door. Gill notes that this was necessary because, having neglected the earlier edict of Cyrus, these Jews needed a fresh grant to leave Persian territory.

**v. 14:** Ezra is “sent by the king and his seven counselors.” The seven counselors are also mentioned in Esther 1:14; they were likely the heads of the seven noble families who aided Darius Hystaspis against the pseudo-Smerdis (Herodotus). Ezra’s mission is “to evaluate Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand” — meaning Ezra carried a copy of the Torah and was to investigate whether the people there were living according to it. This was both a religious and a political fact-finding mission conducted “with regard to the Law.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html)

---

### vv. 15–16 — Silver and Gold for the Temple

The king and his counselors had “freely offered” silver and gold to the God of Israel, “whose dwelling is in Jerusalem.” Ezra was also authorized to collect any additional silver and gold from the province of Babylon, along with freewill offerings from the people and priests. The phrase “whose dwelling is in Jerusalem” reflects the typical Persian diplomatic practice of honouring local deities, though Artaxerxes also speaks of God as “the God of heaven.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

---

### vv. 17–18 — Purchasing Sacrifices; Discretionary Spending

**v. 17:** The money was to be spent “diligently” (or “speedily”) on bulls, rams, lambs, and the accompanying grain and drink offerings — the full sacrificial system according to the Law (cf. Numbers 15). Ellicott observes that “every sacrifice had its own meat-offerings and drink-offerings,” and that “these phrases in the commission of course Ezra dictated.” Gill suggests the king had been “instructed by Ezra, or some other Jew in his court.”

**v. 18:** “You and your brothers may do whatever seems best with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God.” This is a remarkable grant of discretion. Steven Cole (quoted at Precept Austin) notes that Artaxerxes trusted Ezra’s character and integrity so completely that he gave him enormous resources and said, in effect, “use the remainder as you see fit according to God’s will.” Ezra’s obedience was obvious even to a pagan king. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### vv. 19–20 — Temple Vessels and the Royal Treasury

**v. 19:** “You must deliver to the God of Jerusalem all the articles given to you for the service of the house of your God.” These were new vessels offered at this time (see Ezra 8:25), distinct from those returned under Cyrus (Ezra 1:7ff). Kidner suggests they were “a goodwill gift, newly presented.” The word “deliver” means to render complete, full number — nothing was to be held back.

**v. 20:** “If anything else is needed … you may pay for it from the royal treasury.” This is an open-ended provision. Ellicott notes that “every satrap had his local treasury” and this decree gave Ezra very large powers, though vv. 21–22 add qualification by setting limits. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

### vv. 21–22 — Decree to Treasurers West of the Euphrates

Artaxerxes commands all treasurers in the province “beyond the River” (west of the Euphrates) to provide whatever Ezra requires — “promptly” (or “diligently,” “speedily”). The limits are generous: 100 talents of silver (about 3¾ tons, an enormous sum — the same weight of silver Pharaoh Neco imposed as tribute on Judah, 2 Kings 23:33), 100 cors of wheat (about 600 bushels), 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of olive oil (each a bath being about 6 gallons), and salt “without limit” — salt was plentiful near the Dead Sea and used in every offering (Leviticus 2:13). Ellicott observes that “the very restriction seems almost indefinite.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

### v. 23 — The King’s Motive

“Whatever is commanded by the God of heaven must be done diligently for His house. For why should wrath fall on the realm of the king and his sons?” Artaxerxes’ motive was pragmatic and superstitious: like other Persian monarchs, he sought to appease the gods of conquered peoples to protect his throne and dynasty. Enduring Word says: “He believed it was a good and safe policy for his kingdom to do this.” Yet the book of Ezra (and v. 27) makes clear that God sovereignly put this desire into the king’s heart — using a pagan king’s self-interest to accomplish His purposes. “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD; He turns it wherever He wishes” (Proverbs 21:1). Ellicott adds the historical note that in this very year (458 BC), the tide of success turned for Persia against the Athenians in Egypt, which may have encouraged such piety. Artaxerxes, though young, is said to have left eighteen sons — adding weight to “and his sons.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

### v. 24 — Tax Exemption for Temple Personnel

“You have no authority to impose tribute, duty, or toll on any of the priests, Levites, singers, doorkeepers, temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.” This exempted the entire temple ministry from all forms of taxation. Kidner notes that Darius had ordered a similar exemption for cult-servants of Apollo — it was Persian policy to free religious personnel from taxes so they could devote themselves to worship. Gill adds that this was common among the Heathens — the priests of Egypt and the Druids of Britain enjoyed similar privileges. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### v. 25 — Judicial and Teaching Authority

“You, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God which you possess, are to appoint magistrates and judges to judge all the people west of the Euphrates — all who know the laws of your God. And you are to teach these laws to anyone who does not know them.” This makes Ezra supreme over the Jewish population in the entire province. The phrase “the wisdom of your God that is in your hand” may refer to the Law itself (Deuteronomy 4:6) as well as to God-given practical wisdom (cf. Psalm 78:72, where wisdom is “ascribed to the hands”). Some Jewish interpreters took the word “set” as comparative: Ezra’s wisdom exceeded that of the judges. The commission covers both judicial enforcement and catechetical instruction — judges for those who know the law, teaching for those who do not. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html)

### v. 26 — Penalties for Disobedience

“If anyone does not keep the law of your God and the law of the king, let a strict judgment be executed against him, whether death, banishment, confiscation of property, or imprisonment.” Civil authority is added to religious authority. Gill notes that “the law of the king” may refer specifically to this decree giving Jews power to execute their own laws, not the entire Persian legal code. The range of penalties — death, banishment, confiscation, imprisonment — shows the seriousness with which the Persian court viewed religious and civil order. Ellicott observes that “all these powers were usually entrusted to the provincial administrators … but it is obvious that their combination in the one person of this servant of Jehovah demanded express statement.” Enduring Word notes that later passages show Ezra was “primarily a priest and scholar rather than an administrator,” yet the king’s commission gave him courage. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezra/7.htm)

### vv. 27–28 — Ezra’s Doxology

This is the sole expression of Ezra’s private devotion recorded in the narrative, inserted artlessly into the record — Ellicott says this “confirms the impression that the whole narrative is from his hand.” The sudden ejaculatory thanksgiving resembles Nehemiah’s habit.

**v. 27:** “Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who has put into the heart of the king to so honour the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.” Ezra attributes everything to God’s sovereign work in Artaxerxes’ heart — he does not praise the king’s generosity but the God who moved the king. This is consistent with Proverbs 21:1 and the pattern throughout Ezra: God moved Cyrus (1:1), Darius (6:22), and now Artaxerxes (7:27). John Piper (Desiring God) emphasises: “God rules empires … Cyrus and Artaxerxes were not believers. God just directed their hearts to do what he wanted them to get done.” Ligonier’s Reformed devotional adds that Matthew Henry reminds us: “If any good appear to be in our own hearts, or in the hearts of others, we must own it was God that put it there, and bless him for it.” The word “beautify” (or “honour”) is a general term for all that belonged to the restoration and adornment of the temple. [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezra-7.html) | [desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-6](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-6) | [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/piety-of-ezra](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/piety-of-ezra)

**v. 28:** “And who has shown me favour before the king, his counselors, and all his powerful officials.” The Hebrew term translated “favour” (or “mercy,” “steadfast love”) is *chesed*. God’s covenant love extended to Ezra before the highest Persian authorities. “Because the hand of the LORD my God was upon me, I took courage and gathered the leaders of Israel to return with me.” This is the third mention of “the hand of the LORD” in the chapter. God’s blessing moved Ezra from thanksgiving to action — he “gathered leading men” (literally “heads” or “chief men”) to accompany him. Ligonier notes: “When such God-given favour is present, we should take courage as Ezra did, knowing that no weapon fashioned against us shall succeed (Isaiah 54:17).” Steven Cole (Precept Austin) notes: “Ezra didn’t take credit for devoting himself to studying God’s Word or for his bold presentation to the king. He gave all the credit to God for His abundant mercy.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/) | [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary) | [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/piety-of-ezra](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/piety-of-ezra)

## Points of Traditional Difference between Protestant Traditions

### Reformed (Ligonier)
The Reformed reading emphasises **God’s absolute sovereignty over pagan rulers.** Artaxerxes’ decree is not a product of human goodwill but of God “putting” the desire into the king’s heart (v. 27). Ezra is held up as a model for the Reformed principle of *sola scriptura* — reformation begins by returning to Scripture (“to study, to do, to teach”). The threefold pattern in v. 10 is seen as paradigmatic for the church: study, obedience, then teaching — exactly the Reformation pattern. Ligonier also stresses that “the information in the Bible does us no good if it merely stays on the printed page” — private Bible study must lead to application, not mere intellectual knowledge. [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/studying-doing-and-teaching](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/studying-doing-and-teaching) | [learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/artaxerxes-sends-ezra-to-judah](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/artaxerxes-sends-ezra-to-judah)

### Baptist / Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)
Piper uses Ezra 7:27 and the wider Ezra narrative to underscore **God’s providence in geopolitics**: “Cyrus and Artaxerxes were not believers. God just directed their hearts.” He draws on Ezra 7–8 especially to promote fasting as a means of humbling oneself before God (Ezra 8:21–23). The link in Piper’s theology is between God’s sovereign decree (Ezra 7:27) and the human response of dependent prayer and fasting. [desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-6](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-providence-of-god-session-6) | [desiringgod.org/articles/a-call-to-fast-for-humility-and-power](https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-call-to-fast-for-humility-and-power)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik focuses on the **practical, devotional application.** The “hand of the LORD” is understood as God’s tangible blessing and favour that can be sought today. The threefold pattern of v. 10 is “essential for anyone who wants to make a real impact on others with the word of God.” Artaxerxes’ pragmatic, superstitious motives are not hidden — “God used this pagan king’s self-interest to accomplish His purposes” — and believers are encouraged to recognise that “God often works through unlikely circumstances and even the hearts of those who don’t know Him.” [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezra-7/)

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey)
I was unable to fetch content from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the available limits. The Precept Austin compilation does reference the scholarly debate over the chronological relationship between Ezra, Nehemiah, and Artaxerxes I vs. II. R. K. Harrison (Introduction to the Old Testament, pp. 193–197) outlines three theories: (1) Artaxerxes I sent Ezra in 458/457 BC (traditional view); (2) Nehemiah preceded Ezra, who came in 398 BC under Artaxerxes II; (3) the letter dates from the 37th year of Artaxerxes I (428 BC). The traditional view (theory 1) is the one followed by most conservative commentaries. [preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezra-7-commentary)

### Catholic and Orthodox
Searches for content on newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org returned no specific Ezra 7 verse-by-verse material within the available search limit. This gap should be noted. Catholic tradition has historically held Ezra in high regard as a priest-scribe and reformer — the Vulgate treats Ezra and Nehemiah as 1 and 2 Esdras — but specific verse exposition from these sites was not retrievable.
